complaint: A couple of our supporters said they got the same confirmation email twice. Only a handful, not everyone.

response.restated_complaint: A small number of supporters received the same confirmation email twice, while most supporters only got one.

hypotheses.summary: 3 of 29 email messages were sent to the provider twice, exactly 31.0 seconds apart. The trace shows one publish from the orchestrator but two consume events sharing the same parent span in comms-sender, and the second consume carries an SQS receive_count of 2 — meaning the message was never deleted from the queue after the first successful send (which had already returned 202), so it became visible again after the visibility timeout expired and was reprocessed with no idempotency check. This matches the 'handful, not everyone' pattern: only 3 of 29 email sends, spread mostly on one tenant (org-5502, 2 of 3), were affected.
hypotheses.why_this_rank: This is the only finding that directly matches 'same email sent twice to a handful of people' — duplicate provider sends observed on the email channel, exactly the symptom reported.

ruled_out.claim: The duplicates are caused by a subscription/topic misconfiguration or missing consumer (the same mechanism as the push-channel loss).
ruled_out.why_not: The push loss finding (D1.channel_drop.push) describes messages that never reach the provider at all (lost), which is the opposite symptom — no email messages were lost (email delivered 29/29); the duplicate-email issue is a separate mechanism (queue redelivery after send, not a routing/topic drop).

ruled_out.claim: Duplicates could be explained by the sender's SMS provider seam deploy or SDK bump around 2026-03-09/10.
ruled_out.why_not: D2's exemplars (corr-0014, corr-0022, corr-0035) show a consistent 31.0s redelivery pattern tied to queue visibility timeout and missing delete-ack, not to a code deploy; no deploy evidence is cited in D2.

would_resolve: The queue's visibility timeout setting compared to observed send duration, to confirm the delete-ack was simply too slow (delete_failed) versus never issued at all (delete_not_issued)
Sender logs or metrics specifically for delete-message calls and their outcomes, which would distinguish the two competing alternatives attached to D2.duplicate_delivery
